title: OpenAI's 372 math results
lede: On 6 October 2026 OpenAI posted 372 math results from an unreleased model to GitHub, 722 manuscripts in all. Some mathematicians call it good for mathematics; others want the model, the prompts and real review first.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body:
On 6 October 2026, at 6 p.m. EDT, OpenAI posted a GitHub repository of mathematics written by an internal model it has not released [1]. The catalogue holds 722 manuscripts grouped into 372 result families [2]. Each family, the company says, resolves or makes substantial progress on a major open question in mathematics or theoretical computer science [3]. The claims include the four-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and progress toward the [[Riemann hypothesis]] [4].

OpenAI says the model was posed about 4,000 problems over the evaluation, and that each result used three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute on average [5]. Nearly every result came from a single prompt to a single agent, the company says, though some took several attempts [6]. That is a sharp change from September, when one result took a swarm of 10,000 agents [6].

sections.heading: How it got here
sections.body:
The release ends a month of conflict between OpenAI and research mathematicians. On 8 September 2026 OpenAI said an unreleased model had solved the [[Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness|Navier-Stokes]] Millennium Prize problem after 88 hours of work by roughly 10,000 agents [1]. On 10 September the company pulled its sponsorship of a student-run AI maths contest at Caltech, after an open letter signed by 771 mathematicians [2] that called the format "slop mathematics" [3].

On 11 September, 25 Fields Medal winners, [[Terence Tao]] among them, signed a declaration that AI companies' use of math problems as benchmarks harms the field [4]. On 21 September OpenAI said it was assembling an independent advisory group of mathematicians [5], whose recommendations came out on 29 September [6].

sections.heading: Good for mathematics?
sections.body:
OpenAI and some mathematicians argue that putting everything out is better than holding it back. "If we want to know the answers to these math questions, I see no reason why we should ask the company to keep them secret from us," the University of Toronto mathematician Daniel Litt told *Scientific American*. "To me, it's going to be a good thing for mathematics." [1]

OpenAI says it wants to put as powerful a tool as possible in mathematicians' hands [2], and that it cannot slow down because these problems are an indispensable test of whether its AI is getting smarter [3]. It presents the Lean formalizations as the answer to volume: so many results could easily overwhelm the community's capacity for manual review [4]. It also says it will fund workshops and conferences on understanding AI-produced results [5].

sections.heading: What the critics asked for
sections.body:
The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence is hosted at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], and its members include the Fields medalist Timothy Gowers [1]. Its 29 September recommendations drew on more than 600 replies from mathematicians [2]. They ask labs to deposit results in repositories that no AI lab controls [3], to publish for every result the model, the prompts, a summarized chain of thought, the time and the cost [4], and to formalize proofs where possible [5]. The group also says it does not endorse testing advanced problems on proprietary models at all [6].

Measured against that list, the release sits on OpenAI's own GitHub account, names no model and publishes no prompts [7]. OpenAI told *Scientific American* that it takes the guidelines seriously but is not bound by them [8].

sections.heading: What Lean checks
sections.body:
[[Lean (proof assistant)|Lean]] is a programming language that checks a proof's logic by machine [1]. Results verified in it are all but certain to be correct [2]. The repository's formalization catalogue lists 162 papers with a formalized main result [3], out of 722 manuscripts. OpenAI's own README warns that some of the unformalized results could have issues [4].

A Lean check does not answer the question mathematicians care most about. It verifies logical correctness, but it cannot judge whether a result is relevant or original [5]. Deciding whether the proofs hold new and important ideas or are mostly mash-ups of existing techniques will take mathematicians months, *Scientific American* reports [6].

sections.heading: What is next
sections.body:
OpenAI says it is working to release the model as quickly and responsibly as possible [1], and that it is exploring community-hosted repositories for the materials [2]. Corrections will be recorded as new versions, with earlier versions kept online [3]. Many of the new results are not yet understood by OpenAI's own mathematicians, its spokesperson said [4].

The September claim is also still open. As of mid-September the Clay Mathematics Institute still listed Navier-Stokes as unsolved [5]. The Caltech Mathathon that OpenAI left goes ahead from 30 October to 1 November, with Anthropic's credits still in [6].

fights.note: The other side, in the critics' own words.
fights.body:
Many mathematicians say a pile of proofs from a model nobody else can run is not yet mathematics. "Until and unless they release the model and people can replicate their results, I think you should treat any claims about one-shotting problems with a single agent as unverified," said Andrew Sutherland of MIT. "We should ask for receipts." [1]

The advisory group OpenAI convened asked for the model, prompts, time and cost behind each result [2]; OpenAI gave an average compute time and no prompts [3]. Twenty-five Fields medalists wrote that solving problems is only a tool and proxy for understanding [4], and Terence Tao has criticized the "insane" pace of AI labs' results [5].
